title: Clustered Integer Execution Pipeline vs. Centralized Register File
decision: Split the 4-way integer execution engine into two distinct 2-way clusters (Cluster Upper and Cluster Lower), duplicating the integer register file across both clusters.
alternatives_or_rejected: A single centralized integer register file with 8 read ports and 4 write ports supplying all four integer execution units.
rationale: A single 8-read/4-write ported register file would require excessive wire area, long cross-chip routing delays, and high parasitic capacitance that would severely limit the cycle time / target clock frequency.
outcome: Enabled a fast clock frequency by keeping local bypass loops within each cluster fast, accepting a 1-cycle latency penalty for inter-cluster operand transfers.
weakest_point: Exact formal naming of the clusters (e.g., Cluster 0/1 vs Cluster U/L) in the text figure labels.

title: Dual-Bank Instruction Cache Duplication for Multi-Read Bandwidth
decision: Replicate the 64-KB 2-way set-associative I-cache into two identical physical copies (I-Cache Set A and B) to allow reading two instruction fetch blocks simultaneously.
alternatives_or_rejected: Building a multi-ported single-copy instruction cache.
rationale: Multi-porting a single cache array substantially increases cell area, wiring overhead, and access time, whereas replicating the entire array requires less area and achieves lower access latency.
outcome: Allowed fetching up to 4 instructions per cycle across branch boundaries with low access latency.
weakest_point: Exact page location of the instruction cache structure breakdown.

title: Out-of-Order Instruction Scheduling Window Sizing vs Clock Frequency
where_in_paper: Instruction Mapper and Issue / Execution Window
decision: Limit the out-of-order issue queue window size to 80 instructions total (20-entry integer issue queue, 15-entry floating-point issue queue) rather than scaling to a larger monolithic queue.
alternatives_or_rejected: Larger unified issue queues capable of holding more instructions to expose more instruction-level parallelism (ILP).
rationale: Issue queue wake-up and select logic is on the critical timing path; larger queues increase circuit delay and degrade the core clock frequency, which nets worse overall performance.
outcome: Sustained high execution throughput and fast cycle time while maintaining high instruction-level parallelism.
weakest_point: Exact allocation numbers for active instructions versus pending issue queue slots.

title: Speculative Execution with Hardware Memory Orientation / Store Sets
decision: Implement speculative load execution ahead of stores, using a dynamic memory disambiguation prediction mechanism (Store Sets) to predict load-store aliases.
alternatives_or_rejected: Stalling loads until all preceding store addresses are fully calculated and resolved.
rationale: Strictly waiting for store address resolution limits memory-level parallelism; predicting non-aliasing allows memory loads to issue speculatively with high accuracy, recovering via pipeline flush if a misprediction occurs.
outcome: Significantly reduced effective load latency and improved memory pipeline utilization on complex workloads.
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly names the algorithm 'Store Sets' or describes the predictor structurally without using the term 'Store Sets'.

title: Out-of-Order Memory Access Engine with On-Chip L1 Data Cache
decision: Build a 64-KB 2-way set-associative dual-ported L1 data cache using a hit-under-miss non-blocking structure supporting up to 8 outstanding cache misses.
alternatives_or_rejected: Blocking L1 cache structure or single-ported data cache array.
rationale: High-frequency out-of-order instruction execution requires continuous memory supply; blocking on the first L1 cache miss would collapse the out-of-order issue queue.
outcome: Sustained execution around cache misses and provided the necessary load/store memory bandwidth for dual integer/FP pipelines.
weakest_point: Exact maximum count of outstanding L1 data cache misses supported by the MSHR logic.
